docs.title: Process Discovery Case Study: Consulting Firm Client Delivery
docs.text:
From one incomplete discovery call to a documented current-state process, a list of the gaps and the questions to close them, and a prioritized plan for process fixes, automation and AI.

Fictional practice case. The firm and the stakeholder are made up, and this isn't client work. Read the scenario and full transcript →

docs.title: Video walkthrough (9 min)
docs.text:
Download the walkthrough video

I walk through the process, the main gaps, the questions for the next session and the recommendations.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
• What I found: the firm has the right tools (HubSpot, Asana, Google Drive, Slack) and an intended process from lead to billing. At almost every stage, though, what actually happens differs from that intended process. Leads skip HubSpot, work starts before setup, status lives in Slack and email, and time entries come in late.
  • Biggest gaps: no owner was described for the first response to a lead or for the handoff from sales to delivery. "Completion" is never defined, and four key tools were never named.
  • Root cause: the problem is missing rules, owners and connections between tools, not missing software.
  • Recommendation: first define the process and an owner for each stage. Then automate the handoffs: lead capture, project setup when a deal is signed, time-entry reminders, and AI drafts of proposals and client updates that a person reviews.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text: File What it covers 📄 The case Scenario, discovery transcript and brief 1 Discovery analysis 13-stage process summary, inputs and outputs, 9 decision points, 20 information gaps, ownership map, 31 follow-up questions 2 Process documentation Workflow diagram, step-by-step process with owners and systems, decision table, 8 known exceptions (intended vs. actual) 3 Improvement and AI 10 operational challenges, 8 prioritized recommendations, 7 automation and AI opportunities with a rollout order 🗺️ Workflow diagram Workflow as a PNG and as Mermaid source

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
1. Keep facts apart from guesses. Every statement is either what the stakeholder said, an [Assumption], or [Unknown]. Nothing is filled in silently.
  2. Look for the steps nobody described. Between "a client reaches out" and "we have a discovery call", someone has to reply. Between "the client signs" and "the PM sets up the project", someone has to tell the PM. Neither step was described, and both are where leads and context get lost.
  3. Map the intended process against what actually happens. Each stage has an official version and a real one. The gap between them is the main finding, and it runs through all three parts.
  4. Ask questions that build on what was said. The follow-up questions don't repeat what the stakeholder already covered. Each one points back to a numbered gap, and the list ends with real documents to request, because documents show what happens better than interviews do.
  5. Fix the process before automating it. Rules and owners come first. Automation and AI come second, using the tools the firm already pays for, and an AI draft never goes to a client without a person reviewing it.

docs.title: The Case: Scenario, Transcript and Brief
docs.text:
← Back to overview

This is a fictional practice scenario. Michael Reynolds and his firm aren't real, and this isn't client work.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An AI Process Consultant is brought in by a consulting firm that wants to standardize and improve how it delivers client work.

The consultant has finished a first discovery call with a stakeholder. The job now is to analyze what was learned, document the process and find opportunities to improve it.

The transcript is incomplete on purpose. In real engagements, stakeholders rarely give complete information in the first session. The point is to find the gaps, ask good questions, and keep facts and assumptions clearly separate.

docs.title: Discovery transcript
docs.text:
Participants: Michael Reynolds, Managing Partner · Consultant

Consultant: Can you walk me through how a new client engagement starts?

Michael: Most clients come through referrals, LinkedIn, or our website. When someone reaches out, either I or one of our consultants has an initial discovery call to understand their needs.

Sometimes we log the lead in HubSpot right away. Sometimes we don't if it's a referral and we're moving quickly.

Consultant: What happens after the discovery call?

Michael: If it looks like a fit, we prepare a proposal.

Usually I create the proposal, but some senior consultants create their own. The format is mostly the same, although everyone has their own approach.

We send the proposal and wait for approval. Sometimes clients want revisions.

Consultant: Once the proposal is accepted, what happens?

Michael: The client signs an agreement and we schedule a kickoff meeting.

The project manager creates the project in Asana and sets up shared folders.

Well, that's the intended process. Occasionally consultants start work before everything is fully set up because clients want to move quickly.

Consultant: How is work assigned?

Michael: The project manager usually assigns tasks based on consultant availability and expertise.

Although sometimes I assign work directly if it's a high-priority client.

There isn't a formal resource planning system. We mostly track capacity in a spreadsheet.

Consultant: How do you track project progress?

Michael: Most projects are tracked in Asana. Consultants are expected to update tasks weekly.

Some are very good about it. Some provide updates through Slack or email instead.

Consultant: How do clients receive updates?

Michael: Typically through weekly status meetings. Some clients want written reports. Others just want a quick call. It varies quite a bit depending on the engagement.

Consultant: How is billing handled?

Michael: For fixed-fee projects, invoices are usually sent monthly.

For hourly projects, consultants submit time entries and accounting generates invoices. Sometimes time entries come in late, which delays billing.

Consultant: What are your biggest operational challenges?

Michael: Consistency. Different consultants manage projects differently. Documentation isn't always stored in the same place. Sometimes it's in Asana, sometimes Google Drive, sometimes email.

When projects scale, it becomes harder to know whether everyone is following the same process.

Consultant: If you could improve one thing, what would it be?

Michael: I'd want a more standardized delivery process from sales through project completion.

I think we spend too much time coordinating and chasing information instead of delivering value to clients.

End of discovery session.

docs.title: Part 1: Process Discovery Analysis
docs.text:
← Back to overview · Case: scenario and transcript

Labels used: statements from the transcript are facts. Anything inferred is marked [Assumption]. Anything not covered in the session is marked [Unknown]. Gap numbers (e.g. "Gap 9") refer to section 1B in 01-discovery-analysis.md.

docs.title: Purpose of the process
docs.text:
Take a potential client from first contact to a signed engagement, deliver the work, keep the client informed and bill for it.

Michael's goal: one standard delivery process "from sales through project completion", so the team spends less time coordinating and chasing information and more time delivering value.

docs.title: Key stakeholders
docs.text:
Stakeholder Role in the process (as described) Michael Reynolds, Managing Partner Runs some discovery calls, usually writes the proposal, sometimes assigns work directly for high-priority clients Consultants Run some discovery calls, deliver the work, are expected to update Asana weekly, submit time entries on hourly projects Senior consultants Sometimes write their own proposals Project manager (PM) Creates the project in Asana, sets up shared folders, usually assigns tasks by availability and expertise Accounting Generates invoices for hourly projects from time entries Client Reaches out, joins the discovery call, approves or asks to revise the proposal, signs the agreement, receives updates

Not named [Unknown]: who watches incoming inquiries and replies first, and who sends fixed-fee invoices.

docs.title: Systems and tools referenced
docs.text:
Tool Used for (as described) Consistency HubSpot Logging leads Not always used. Fast-moving referrals are sometimes not logged Asana Projects, tasks, progress tracking, some documentation Some consultants update through Slack or email instead Shared folders Project files, set up by the PM Location not named. Google Drive [Assumption] Google Drive Some documentation One of three places documents end up Spreadsheet Tracking consultant capacity ("mostly") No formal resource planning system Slack Informal progress updates Used in place of Asana by some consultants Email Progress updates and some documentation Used in place of Asana by some consultants LinkedIn and the website Lead sources (with referrals)

Never named [Unknown]: the proposal tool, the agreement or e-signature tool, the time-tracking tool and the invoicing or accounting system.

docs.title: Major process stages
docs.text:
1. Lead arrives: "most clients" reach out through a referral, LinkedIn or the website. All of this is inbound. Outbound sales was not mentioned.
  2. First response and scheduling [Unknown]: someone must reply to the inquiry and book the discovery call. Who does this, through which channel and how fast was not covered. The HubSpot entry, if made, probably happens here [Assumption].
  3. Discovery call: Michael or a consultant learns the client's needs.
  4. Fit decision: "if it looks like a fit", a proposal is prepared.
  5. Proposal: usually written by Michael, sometimes by a senior consultant. "The format is mostly the same, although everyone has their own approach."
  6. Proposal review: the proposal is sent, then the firm waits for approval. Sometimes the client asks for revisions.
  7. Agreement: the client signs an agreement.
  8. Handoff, kickoff and project setup: a kickoff meeting is scheduled (by whom is [Unknown]) and the PM creates the Asana project and shared folders. How the PM learns the deal is signed, and the order of these steps, are [Unknown]. This is the "intended process". Consultants sometimes start work before setup is finished.
  9. Work assignment: the PM usually assigns tasks by availability and expertise, using the capacity spreadsheet. Michael sometimes assigns directly for high-priority clients.
  10. Delivery and progress tracking: consultants are expected to update Asana weekly. Some update through Slack or email instead.
  11. Client updates: typically weekly status meetings. Some clients want written reports, others a quick call.
  12. Billing: fixed-fee projects are usually invoiced monthly. On hourly projects, consultants submit time entries and accounting generates invoices. Sometimes time entries come in late, which delays billing.
  13. Completion [Unknown]: named as the end of the process but never described. It could mean the final deliverable is accepted, the contract term ends or the final invoice is paid. It likely differs between fixed-fee and hourly work.

docs.title: Decision points
docs.text:
1. Log the lead in HubSpot? Sometimes skipped when it's a referral and "we're moving quickly". There is no rule.
  2. Who runs the discovery call? Michael or a consultant. The criteria are [Unknown].
  3. Is the client a fit? If yes, a proposal is prepared. The fit criteria and what happens to a no-fit lead are [Unknown].
  4. Who writes the proposal? Usually Michael, sometimes a senior consultant. When each one does is [Unknown].
  5. Does the client accept the proposal? Accept leads to the agreement. Revisions loop back to the proposal. Rejection is [Unknown].
  6. Start work before setup is complete? Happens when the client wants to move quickly. Who allows it is [Unknown].
  7. Who assigns the work? Usually the PM. Michael for high-priority clients. "High priority" is not defined.
  8. What update format does the client get? Meeting, written report or call. Who decides, and when, is [Unknown].
  9. Fixed fee or hourly? Decides the billing path: a monthly invoice, or invoicing from time entries.

docs.title: Missing information (not covered in the session)
docs.text: # Stage What we don't know Why it matters 1 First response Who watches the inbound channels (website form, LinkedIn, referral emails), and how fast they reply A slow first reply loses leads. With no owner, it's nobody's job to reply 2 Lead tracking Lead volume per month, and how many leads never reach HubSpot Shows how large the HubSpot gap is and whether pipeline reports can be trusted 3 Discovery call Whether notes are taken, in what format and where they're stored The proposal and the delivery team both depend on what was learned on this call 4 Fit decision The criteria for a fit (budget, service type, size, timing) and what happens to no-fit leads Without criteria, two people can judge the same lead differently 5 Proposal Whether a template exists, how pricing is set, who reviews or approves before sending, and the tool used "Mostly the same format" could mean a shared template or just habit 6 Proposal review Typical number of revision rounds, how long approval takes, follow-up when a client goes quiet, rejection handling Shows where deals stall 7 Agreement Who drafts the agreement, whether it's a standard contract or custom, and the signature tool The signed agreement is what's meant to start project setup 8 Handoff How the PM learns a deal is signed, and what information is passed from sales to delivery This is the point where client context is most likely to get lost 9 Kickoff Who schedules and runs it, the agenda, and whether it comes before or after Asana and folder setup The order in the transcript is unclear 10 Early starts How often work starts before setup, and what's missing when it does (Asana project, folders, signed agreement?) The transcript only says "before everything is fully set up". If that can include before the agreement is signed, it's a billing and legal risk 11 Assignment What the capacity spreadsheet tracks, who updates it and how often Assignments are only as good as this spreadsheet 12 Progress tracking What a complete weekly Asana update includes, whether anyone checks it, and why some consultants prefer Slack or email Expectations without a check, or Asana being harder to use, may explain the drift [Assumption]. The fix depends on which one it is 13 Client updates Who prepares reports, who decides the format, and whether it's set at kickoff The work behind each update format is unknown 14 Billing The time-tracking and invoicing tools, the time-entry deadline, who sends fixed-fee invoices, how payment is collected and followed up Late time entries already delay billing 15 Completion What "complete" means (deliverables accepted, final invoice paid, contract end), and any closeout steps: sign-off, final report, file archive, feedback Michael wants a process "through project completion", but that end point isn't defined 16 Scale Team size: number of consultants, PMs and accounting staff, and the number of active projects Changes which fixes make sense 17 Engagement types Fixed-fee vs. hourly split, and whether other types exist (retainers, milestone billing) Billing and completion depend on the type 18 Documentation Which documents a project produces (proposal, agreement, notes, reports, deliverables) and where each is supposed to live Michael named scattered documentation as a core problem, but no standard was described to measure against 19 Baseline metrics Any current numbers: time from inquiry to proposal, proposal win rate, invoice delay, hours per week spent coordinating Without a baseline, the effect of any improvement can't be shown 20 Changes during delivery How scope changes, extra work, pauses or cancellations are handled and approved Common in consulting and directly affects billing. Not mentioned at all

docs.title: Unclear responsibilities or ownership
docs.text: Activity Who it could be What's unclear Replying to new inquiries Michael, a consultant or someone else Not mentioned at all Running the discovery call "Either I or one of our consultants" How it's decided Logging leads in HubSpot Whoever takes the call [Assumption] No one is named, and skipping is allowed Writing the proposal Michael, usually. Senior consultants, sometimes When a senior consultant writes it, and whether Michael reviews it Approving pricing and terms Michael [Assumption] Not discussed Telling the PM a deal is signed Unknown No handoff owner Allowing an early start Unknown It "happens". No one is named as approving it Assigning work PM, usually. Michael for high-priority clients Who decides a client is "high priority", and whether the PM is told when Michael assigns directly Keeping the capacity spreadsheet current Unknown Not discussed Making sure Asana is updated PM [Assumption] "Consultants are expected to", but no one enforces it Preparing client updates and reports PM or consultant [Assumption] Not discussed Chasing late time entries Unknown Late entries delay billing, but no one is named to chase them Sending fixed-fee invoices Accounting [Assumption] Only hourly invoicing is tied to accounting Deciding a project is complete Unknown Not discussed Owning the overall process Michael [Assumption] No process owner is named

docs.title: Assumptions I'm making (not yet validated)
docs.text:
1. The shared folders the PM creates are in Google Drive.
  2. The proposal is based on what was learned in the discovery call.
  3. Michael approves pricing and terms, including proposals written by senior consultants.
  4. The kickoff meeting includes the client.
  5. The fixed-fee monthly invoice amount comes from the signed agreement.
  6. Accounting is a person or team separate from the consultants.
  7. Asana and Google Drive are the intended homes for project tracking and documents. Slack and email are workarounds.
  8. The engagement types are fixed-fee and hourly only.
  9. "Completion" happens once per project, not per phase or deliverable.
  10. The firm is small enough that Michael is involved in day-to-day decisions. He writes most proposals and assigns some work himself.

docs.title: 1C. Follow-Up Questions
docs.text: These are for a 45 to 60 minute follow-up session. Each question builds on something Michael already told us, and the gap numbers point back to 1B. Ideally the PM, one consultant and someone from accounting join for part of the session, since several answers sit with them.

docs.title: Lead intake and first response
docs.text:
1. When an inquiry comes in through the website or LinkedIn, where does it land, and who sees it first? (Gap 1)
  2. Who replies and books the discovery call? Roughly how long does that take today? (Gap 1)
  3. About how many new inquiries do you get in a month? How many of them come from referrals? (Gap 2)
  4. When a referral moves fast and skips HubSpot, does it ever get added later? If not, how do you know what's in your pipeline? (Gap 2)

docs.title: Discovery and fit
docs.text:
1. How do you decide whether you or a consultant takes the discovery call? (Ownership)
  2. What makes a client "a fit"? Can you give a recent example of one you turned down, and why? (Gap 4)
  3. What happens to a lead that isn't a fit? Do you refer them elsewhere, keep them in HubSpot, or drop them? (Gap 4)
  4. Are notes from the discovery call written down? If so, where do they live, and who reads them later? (Gap 3)

docs.title: Proposal and agreement
docs.text:
1. You said the format is "mostly the same". Is there a shared template, or do people start from an old proposal? (Gap 5)
  2. How is pricing set, and how is fixed-fee vs. hourly chosen? Who signs off on the price before a proposal goes out? (Gap 5, Gap 17)
  3. When a senior consultant writes a proposal, do you review it before it's sent? (Ownership)
  4. On average, how many revision rounds does a proposal go through, and how long until a client decides? What do you do when a client goes quiet? (Gap 6)
  5. Who prepares the agreement? Is it a standard contract, and which tool is used for signatures? (Gap 7)

docs.title: Handoff, kickoff and setup
docs.text:
1. Once a client signs, how does the PM find out? What information do they get from whoever sold the deal? (Gap 8)
  2. Does kickoff happen before or after the Asana project and folders are set up? Who runs it? (Gap 9)
  3. When consultants start early, what's usually missing: Asana, folders, the kickoff, or even the signed agreement? Who agrees to the early start? (Gap 10)
  4. Roughly how often does work start before setup is complete? (Gap 10)

docs.title: Assignment and capacity
docs.text:
1. What does the capacity spreadsheet track (hours, projects, skills)? Who updates it, and how often? (Gap 11)
  2. What makes a client "high priority"? When you assign work directly, is the PM told, and does the spreadsheet get updated? (Ownership)

docs.title: Delivery, tracking and client updates
docs.text:
1. What should a weekly Asana update include? Does anyone check that it happened? (Gap 12)
  2. Why do some consultants send updates through Slack or email instead? Is something about Asana getting in the way? (Gap 12)
  3. Where is each type of document supposed to live, such as notes, deliverables and client reports? (Gap 18)
  4. Who decides the client update format, and when? Who writes the written reports, and roughly how long does each one take? (Gap 13)

docs.title: Billing and completion
docs.text:
1. Which tools do you use for time tracking and invoicing? (Gap 14)
  2. Is there a deadline for time entries? When they're late, who chases them, and how long does that usually delay an invoice? (Gap 14)
  3. Who sends fixed-fee invoices, and who follows up on unpaid invoices? (Gap 14, Ownership)
  4. How do you know a project is finished? Is there a client sign-off, a final invoice, or a closeout step such as archiving files or asking for feedback? Is it different for fixed-fee and hourly projects? (Gap 15)

docs.title: Scale and priorities
docs.text:
1. How many consultants, PMs and accounting staff do you have, and how many projects are usually active at once? (Gap 16)
  2. Where do you feel the most time is lost to coordinating and chasing? Do you have any numbers, even rough ones? (Gap 19)
  3. When a client asks for extra work or the scope changes mid-project, what happens? Who approves it, and how does it reach billing? (Gap 20)
  4. Who would own a standardized process once it's defined? (Ownership)

docs.title: Documents to request before the next session
docs.text:
• 2 or 3 recent proposals from different authors, to see how much the format really varies
  • A sample agreement
  • A view of the capacity spreadsheet
  • Two active Asana projects: one well kept, and one that isn't
  • A recent client status report
  • A recent invoice and the time entries behind it, for an hourly project

No standard for updates E7 Time entries arrive on time Time entries sometimes come in late Hourly invoicing is delayed, which affects cash flow [Assumption] E8 Documents in one place Spread across Asana, Google Drive and email Time lost searching. Risk when people leave

docs.title: Areas that need clarification
docs.text: These are covered in full in 1B and 1C. In priority order: 1. First response and handoff (steps 2 and 9): no owner, so leads and client context can be lost. 2. Completion and payment collection (step 16): the end of the process is undefined. 3. Early starts (E3): how often it happens, and whether it ever happens before the agreement is signed. 4. Unnamed tools (proposal, e-signature, time tracking, invoicing): needed before any automation can be designed. 5. Decision rules (D2, D3, D4, D6, D7, D8): each depends on someone's judgement, with no written rule. 6. Who owns client updates and fixed-fee invoices (steps 14, 15a).

docs.title: Part 3: Process Improvement and AI Opportunities
docs.text:
← Back to overview · Case: scenario and transcript

Labels used: statements from the transcript are facts. Anything inferred is marked [Assumption]. Anything not covered in the session is marked [Unknown]. Gap numbers (e.g. "Gap 9") refer to section 1B in 01-discovery-analysis.md.

docs.title: 3A. Operational Challenges
docs.text:
Ordered by business impact. Each one traces back to the transcript.

# Challenge Evidence from discovery Risk C1 No single process owner, and no checks at handoffs Responsibilities shift case by case (proposals, assignment, setup, updates). No one checks that steps happen This is the root cause behind most of the items below. The process depends on individual habits C2 Late time entries delay billing "Sometimes time entries come in late, which delays billing" Cash flow and revenue. This is the only issue Michael tied directly to money C3 No clean sales-to-delivery handoff No handoff described. Work sometimes starts before Asana and folders exist Client context gets lost. Work isn't tracked from day one. Possible unbilled or unapproved work if it ever starts before signing [Assumption] C4 Project status is spread across Asana, Slack and email "Some provide updates through Slack or email instead" The PM and Michael have no single view of where projects stand. Time is spent chasing updates C5 Documents have no single home "Sometimes it's in Asana, sometimes Google Drive, sometimes email" Time lost searching. Knowledge is lost when people leave. Harder to onboard new consultants C6 Incomplete pipeline data Fast referrals are sometimes not logged in HubSpot Pipeline reports can't be trusted. Lead history and follow-ups can be lost C7 Proposals vary by author "Everyone has their own approach". Michael writes most of them Inconsistent client experience. Michael is a bottleneck on new revenue C8 Capacity is managed in a spreadsheet, outside the main tools No resource planning system. Michael sometimes assigns work directly Over- or under-allocation. The spreadsheet may not reflect Michael's direct assignments [Assumption] C9 Client updates aren't standardized Meetings, written reports or calls, depending on the client Different effort for each client, and no guaranteed level of service C10 Undefined start and end of the process First response and completion were never described Leads can go unanswered. Projects may never be formally closed, signed off or archived

The common thread: the tools are already in place (HubSpot, Asana, Drive, Slack). What's missing is rules, owners and connections between those tools. That's good news, because most fixes don't need new software.

docs.title: 3B. Improvement Recommendations
docs.text:
Process fixes come first, because automating an undefined process just makes the inconsistency happen faster.

Priority Recommendation Fixes Effort 1. Now Define the standard process and name an owner for each stage. Use the workflow in Task 2 as the starting point, validate it in the next session, and assign one owner per stage (first response, handoff, setup, client updates, billing follow-up, closeout) C1, C3, C10 Low 2. Now Set four non-negotiable rules: (1) every lead goes into HubSpot, (2) no work starts until the Asana project exists, or the PM approves an early start, (3) Asana is where project status lives, (4) time entries are due by a fixed day each week C3, C4, C6, C2 Low 3. Now One document standard: a fixed Google Drive folder template for every client (Sales / Contract / Delivery / Reports / Billing), linked from the Asana project. Nothing lives only in email C5 Low 4. Next A sales-to-delivery handoff checklist: signed agreement, scope, billing type, client contacts, update preference and discovery notes. The PM confirms it before kickoff C3, C9 Low 5. Next A standard proposal template with fixed sections and pricing blocks. Authors keep their own voice in the summary only C7 Medium 6. Next Agree the client update format at kickoff (one of three standard options) and record it in Asana C9 Low 7. Later Define "complete" for fixed-fee and hourly projects, with a closeout checklist: client sign-off, final invoice, files archived, feedback requested C10 Low 8. Later Move capacity tracking into Asana, or a tool connected to it, once the rules above are working, so direct assignments show up automatically C8 Medium

How to measure it: set a baseline first (1B, Gap 19). Then track time from inquiry to first reply, the share of leads in HubSpot, days from month end to invoice, how many projects are set up before work starts, and how many projects have their documents in the standard folder.

docs.title: 3C. Automation and AI Opportunities
docs.text: These build on the rules in 3B and use the tools the firm already has. The connections could be built in a workflow tool such as n8n, Zapier or Make, which all connect to HubSpot, Asana, Google Drive and Slack. The final choice depends on the tools not yet named (1B, Gap 14).

docs.title: 1. Automatic lead capture and first response
docs.text:
• Current problem: referrals sometimes skip HubSpot. Nobody owns the first reply, and response speed is unknown.
  • Proposed solution: website form and LinkedIn inquiries create a HubSpot record automatically. For referrals, a forwarding address or a Slack command creates the record in seconds. AI drafts a short first reply and suggests discovery call times for the owner to review and send. If an inquiry has no reply after an agreed window, a Slack alert goes out.
  • Expected impact: every lead is tracked, first replies are faster, and pipeline reports can be trusted.
  • Assumptions: inquiries arrive in channels that can be connected (form, email). LinkedIn messages may still need manual entry. The firm agrees on a response-time target.

docs.title: 2. AI discovery call summary
docs.text:
• Current problem: we don't know whether discovery notes are recorded or where (1B, Gap 3). The proposal author and the delivery team depend on them.
  • Proposed solution: record the call (with client consent), transcribe it, and have AI produce a structured summary: needs, scope, budget signals, timeline and fit indicators. The summary is saved to the HubSpot deal and later passed on in the handoff.
  • Expected impact: client context is captured once and reused. Proposals start from real notes, and fit decisions are easier to compare.
  • Assumptions: clients consent to recording, and calls happen on a platform that supports it (Zoom, Meet or Teams).

docs.title: 3. AI-assisted proposal drafting
docs.text:
• Current problem: proposals vary by author, and Michael writes most of them, so they wait on him.
  • Proposed solution: combine the standard template (3B, item 5) with an AI first draft built from the discovery summary and past winning proposals. The author edits, and Michael reviews a consistent draft instead of writing from scratch.
  • Expected impact: faster proposals, a consistent format, and senior consultants can take on more proposals with less of Michael's time.
  • Assumptions: past proposals are available to learn from, and pricing rules can be written down. A person always reviews before anything is sent.

docs.title: 4. Automatic project setup when the deal is signed
docs.text:
• Current problem: no defined handoff. Setup is manual, and work sometimes starts before it's done.
  • Proposed solution: when the HubSpot deal is marked "Closed Won", or the e-signature completes, an automation creates the Asana project from a template, creates the standard Drive folder, links the two, posts the handoff checklist to the PM in Slack, and drafts the kickoff invite.
  • Expected impact: setup takes minutes instead of depending on someone's free time. Early starts become less likely to happen without setup, because the setup is already there.
  • Assumptions: deal status in HubSpot is kept up to date. The e-signature tool (not yet named) can trigger the automation.

docs.title: 5. Status updates captured in one place, plus AI client reports
docs.text:
• Current problem: status is split across Asana, Slack and email, and client reports are written by hand in different formats.
  • Proposed solution: (a) A weekly Slack nudge to each consultant links to their open Asana tasks. Updates posted in a project's Slack channel are added to Asana automatically. (b) AI drafts each client's weekly update from Asana activity, in the format agreed at kickoff (meeting agenda, written report or call notes). The PM reviews and sends it.
  • Expected impact: a single view of status for the PM and Michael, less chasing, and consistent client updates with less writing.
  • Assumptions: the firm accepts Asana as the single source of status. Project Slack channels exist or can be created.

docs.title: 6. Time-entry reminders and invoice preparation
docs.text:
• Current problem: late time entries delay hourly billing.
  • Proposed solution: automated Slack reminders before the weekly deadline, a personal follow-up for anyone still missing entries, and a weekly report to the PM of projects with missing time. When entries are complete, invoice drafts are created for accounting to review. Fixed-fee invoices are drafted automatically each month from the agreement terms.
  • Expected impact: fewer late entries, faster invoicing and better cash flow. This is the most directly measurable win.
  • Assumptions: the time-tracking and invoicing tools (not yet named) have APIs or exports. A weekly deadline is agreed in 3B.

docs.title: 7. Operations dashboard and AI weekly digest
docs.text:
• Current problem: "When projects scale, it becomes harder to know whether everyone is following the same process."
  • Proposed solution: a simple dashboard that pulls from HubSpot and Asana, showing open leads with no reply, proposals waiting, projects missing setup, overdue Asana updates, missing time entries and capacity. Each Monday, AI writes a short digest for Michael that highlights exceptions only.
  • Expected impact: Michael can see in a few minutes whether the process is being followed, without chasing people.
  • Assumptions: recommendations 1 to 6 are in place, so the data exists. Team size makes a dashboard worthwhile (1B, Gap 16).

docs.title: Suggested order
docs.text:
1. Weeks 1 to 2: 3B rules and owners, plus quick automations #1 (lead capture) and #6 (time-entry reminders). These are low effort and the impact is visible right away.
  2. Weeks 3 to 6: #4 (project setup) and #5 (status capture and client reports), after the handoff checklist and folder template are agreed.
  3. Later: #2 and #3 (AI on discovery calls and proposals) and #7 (dashboard), once the data and templates are consistent.

Principle throughout: AI drafts and people approve. Nothing goes to a client without review.
